overview.title: 📖 Overview: Gentiles, Misuse, and Lashes Without an Action
overview.subtitle: Temurah 3a–3b
overview.hebrewSource: כׇּל לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה בַּתּוֹרָה, עָשָׂה בָּהּ מַעֲשֶׂה — חַיָּיב, לֹא עָשָׂה בָּהּ מַעֲשֶׂה — פָּטוּר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by closing (unresolved, as teiku) Rami bar Ḥama's dilemma about a gentile who consecrates an offering that a Jew then brings for atonement. It then works through the baraita's list of halakhot that do not apply to gentiles' consecrated animals — misuse, piggul, notar, tumah, and temurah — each traced to its own verse, with Rabbi Yosei dissenting about property consecrated for Temple maintenance. The Gemara then turns to Rav's broad principle that a prohibition violated without a physical action carries no lashes, and lists its exceptions: oaths, substitution, and cursing another with God's name. A long analysis of oaths about the past versus the future follows, asking exactly which false statements are punished.

slides.title: 🌍 A Gentile's Offering, a Jew's Atonement
slides.subtitle: Rami bar Ḥama's dilemma is left as teiku

nodes.content: ❓ A gentile consecrates an animal, but a Jew achieves atonement with it — who controls whether it can undergo temurah?
📌 Rabbi Yoḥanan's case (teruma of another's produce) is different: it 'comes by the power of a Jew' start to finish

columns.label: Follow the consecrator
columns.content: The gentile consecrated it — he cannot effect substitution, so no one can

columns.label: Follow the one atoning
columns.content: The Jew achieves atonement with it — perhaps he can effect substitution

nodes.content: ⏳ תֵּיקוּ — the dilemma stands unresolved: must the animal be in the possession of someone able to effect substitution from start to end?

callout.label: Note:
callout.text: This teiku leaves open whether temurah requires continuous ownership by a person legally capable of it.

slides.title: 🚫 What a Gentile's Consecrated Animal Is Exempt From
slides.subtitle: Each exemption is traced to its own verse via verbal analogy (gezeirah shavah)
rows: General caution, not a Torah verse
'Sin'–'sin' analogy to teruma (Lev. 5:15 / 22:9), which says 'children of Israel' — not gentiles
Leviticus 22:2 names 'holy items of the children of Israel'; further linked via 'profane'–'profane' and 'iniquity'–'iniquity'
Gentiles cannot effect substitution at all
'He shall not substitute it' (Lev. 27:10) follows the opening words 'Speak to the children of Israel' (Lev. 27:2)

callout.label: Second source for temurah:
callout.text: Alternatively: substitution of an animal is juxtaposed to the animal tithe, which is juxtaposed to the grain tithe — and the grain tithe verse (Numbers 18:24) says 'children of Israel,' not gentiles.

slides.title: 🏛️ Rabbi Yosei's Stringency
slides.subtitle: Not all consecrated property of a gentile is treated the same

boxes.title: Kodshei Mizbe'ach (altar offerings)
items: Sanctity inheres in the animal's body (kedushat haguf), like teruma
No liability for misuse of a gentile's offering

boxes.title: Kodshei Bedek HaBayit (Temple upkeep)
items: Sanctity inheres in the item's value (kedushat damim) — it will be sold
One is liable for misuse, even of a gentile's donation

callout.label: Rabbi Yosei says:
callout.text: 'With regard to all of them I see fit to be stringent' — reading Leviticus 22:18 as equating a gentile's ('stranger's') offering fully with a Jew's.

slides.title: 🚷 Rav's Rule: No Action, No Lashes — Except Three
slides.subtitle: Rav Yehuda cites Rav; Rabbi Yosei HaGelili via Rabbi Yoḥanan lists the exceptions

steps.content: 1️⃣ General principle: for any Torah prohibition, if one transgressed with a physical act, he is flogged; without an act, he is exempt
2️⃣ Challenge: temurah involves no action (only speech), yet the mishna flogs the substituter!
3️⃣ Answer: our mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds a 'prohibition without an action' is flogged — though it disagrees with him about the inheritor
4️⃣ Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's list of true exceptions to the general rule: one who takes an oath, one who effects temurah, and one who curses another using God's name — all flogged despite no action

callout.label: Rabbi Yoḥanan's refinement:
callout.text: Don't actually list temurah among the 'no-action' exceptions — speech itself performs an act of consecration in that case.

slides.title: 🤥 Which False Oaths Bring Lashes?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yoḥanan, Reish Lakish, and Rabbi Abbahu narrow the case

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: If a false oath about the future ('I will eat this loaf today') goes unfulfilled, is the oath-taker flogged? We learned that Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish both say: he is not flogged!

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: Not flogged, because it is a prohibition without an action — and no prohibition without an action brings lashes.

lines.speaker: Reish Lakish
lines.text: Not flogged, but for a different reason: there was only an uncertain forewarning (no single moment of transgression).

lines.speaker: R' Abbahu
lines.text: So what false oath does bring lashes without an action? It must be about the past: 'I swear I ate it' (when he didn't), or 'I swear I did not eat it' (when he did).

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: The Torah explicitly likens a false oath (שֶׁקֶר) to an oath in vain (שָׁוְא) — just as 'in vain' refers to the past, so must the false oath that is flogged.

callout.label: Conclusion:
callout.text: Only a false oath about a past fact is punished by lashes without an accompanying action; an unfulfilled future oath is not.

summary.principle: A gentile's consecrated animal is exempt from misuse, piggul, notar, tumah, and temurah by Torah law; and while most 'action-less' prohibitions carry no lashes, oaths, substitution, and cursing with God's name are the exceptions.

flowSteps.content: 🌍 Teiku: whose 'ownership' governs a gentile-consecrated, Jewish-atoned offering?
🚫 Gentile's offering exempt from misuse/piggul/notar/tumah (Torah level) via verbal analogies to teruma

columns.content: 🐐 Two sources exclude gentiles from temurah entirely
🏛️ R' Yosei: still liable for misuse of bedek habayit property

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: no action, no lashes — except oaths, temurah, and cursing with God's Name

quiz.q: How does the Gemara leave Rami bar Ḥama's dilemma about a gentile-consecrated, Jewish-atoned offering?
o: It rules that the consecrator always controls substitution
It rules that the one achieving atonement always controls substitution
It is left unresolved as teiku
It rules the animal may never be sacrificed
quiz.e: The Gemara explicitly concludes 'תֵּיקוּ' — the question of whether continuous ownership by someone capable of substitution is required remains unresolved.

quiz.q: By what level of law is a gentile's consecrated animal exempt from the prohibition of misuse (me'ilah)?
o: It is not exempt at all
By rabbinic law only
By Torah law, via a 'sin'-'sin' verbal analogy to teruma
Only if the gentile converts
quiz.e: The Gemara states that deriving benefit ab initio is forbidden only rabbinically, while liability for misuse after the fact is waived by Torah law, derived by verbal analogy from teruma's verse naming 'the children of Israel.'

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yosei, for which consecrated items of a gentile IS one liable for misuse?
o: None — he agrees fully with Rabbi Shimon
Only altar offerings (kodshei mizbe'ach)
Only items consecrated for Temple maintenance (kodshei bedek habayit)
Only libations
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei distinguishes: the 'sin'-'sin' exemption applies only to items with inherent bodily sanctity like teruma (altar offerings); items whose sanctity is monetary (bedek habayit) remain subject to misuse liability.

quiz.q: According to Rav (via Rav Yehuda), what is the general rule about lashes for violating a Torah prohibition?
o: Lashes always apply regardless of action
Lashes apply only if the transgression involved a physical action; without an action, one is exempt
Lashes never apply to prohibitions
Lashes apply only to positive commandments
quiz.e: Rav's rule is that a prohibition transgressed through action incurs lashes, while one transgressed without any action does not — subject to specific named exceptions.

quiz.q: Which three transgressions did Rabbi Yosei HaGelili list as exceptions where lashes apply even without a physical action?
o: Theft, murder, and idolatry
Taking an oath, effecting substitution (temurah), and cursing another using God's name
Eating pig, mixing wool and linen, and working on Shabbat
Not eating matzah, not sitting in a sukkah, and not hearing the shofar
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's list (via Rabbi Yoḥanan) names one who swears falsely, one who effects temurah, and one who curses another with God's name — though Rabbi Yoḥanan later says temurah should not really be listed, since speech itself constitutes an act there.
